observations.text: Rowan has anxiety about resuming work responsibilities.
Rowan avoids tasks and communication.
Affect was subdued but responsive, especially when discussing their partner's support.
Rowan presents with depressed mood.
Rowan sought care for several weeks of low mood, reduced interest, fragmented sleep, and worry about returning to work after a leave.
No immediate safety concern was identified; Rowan could discuss support contacts and ways to seek help.
Rowan reported waking in the night and then checking the time repeatedly.
Rowan has sleep disruption.
Rowan delayed replying to a work message for fear of being asked for a firm return date.
Rowan was quiet at first, then took part relevantly and appeared receptive to peer suggestions.
Patient arrived late after parking difficulty and had to leave early for a previously arranged ride.
The group focused on recognizing early physical signs of anxiety and choosing a coping response before withdrawing from a task.
Patient did not check in for the scheduled individual visit and was marked no-show; outreach calls followed.
Patient reported a poor night of sleep, which they said contributed to the morning getting away from them.
Rowan described partner reminders as evidence that they were falling behind, while Casey said the reminders were meant to help but increased tension.
Rowan felt watched when asked repeatedly whether they had contacted work; Casey worried that giving space might leave them isolated.
Rowan remained present and engaged and became more animated describing a shared evening walk as support that did not feel like pressure.
The rehearsal became less defensive with repetition, and both partners contributed ideas for a brief, predictable check-in.
The couple chose an evening walk as a shared activity that avoids discussing progress, which Rowan found more acceptable than a lengthy task review.
Family session focused on patterns of support at home as Rowan attempts to rebuild a routine.
The family session was for communication practice about slowing down an anxious exchange around return-to-work.
Rowan reported that a weekend walk with Casey helped the evening feel less dominated by worry.
Rowan described leaving work messages unopened and identified looking at one message as a lower step than replying to all.
Patient checked in before the group began and stayed until release; no transport concern was reported.
Rowan wrote down an action to try after breakfast and asked how to respond if the morning went poorly.
Group addressed behavioral activation and the difference between an activity being possible and it feeling easy.
Mood was described as somewhat less heavy on days with a planned activity, with ongoing concern about work communication.
Rowan attended for medication management addressing medication use, tolerability, adherence, and symptom response.
Rowan reported continuing sleep interruption and daytime tiredness.
Rowan has not yet replied to a work message and continues to imagine being asked questions they cannot answer.
Affect was more varied than at intake, although worry was evident when discussing employment.
Session focused on the prediction behind a delayed work reply and drafting a short acknowledgment.
Sleep remains interrupted and getting started in the morning continues to require effort.
The coping skills group on January 15 was cancelled by the clinic because of staff illness.
Thinking about work continues to make Rowan want to put things off; persistent avoidance remains.
Ongoing avoidance of work communication.
Casey reported Rowan had been getting out for short walks and seemed more willing to discuss the coming week.
Rowan says getting out of the apartment has become a little easier.
Casey described Rowan becoming quiet when conversation turns to work, and mornings remain difficult.
PHQ-9 total of 14 is lower than the intake score of 18 recorded on January 5.
Clinician review notes some improvement in depressive symptoms.
Rowan describes sleep as inconsistent, with sleep disruption still clinically relevant.
Sleep is inconsistent.
When discussion turned to returning to the workplace, Rowan became visibly tense and said the discussion felt difficult to manage.
Patient identified anxiety about reconnecting with work.
Rowan felt overwhelmed by workplace demands discussed in group and reported that immediate anxiety eased enough to discuss a next step.
Rowan identified postponing a message to a supervisor as a familiar pattern.
Persistent avoidance and disrupted sleep continue to interfere with resuming a usual work routine.
Patient attended the opening check-in, accepted the exercise handout, and asked for more help from the individual clinician.
Skills group addressed the sequence of trigger, anxious prediction, physical activation, and avoidance.
Patient attended the group's opening check-in and later requested additional individual help.
Rowan became anxious during group and needed individual grounding and review of coping strategies.
Rowan denied current suicidal thoughts and no acute safety concern was identified.
Patient repeatedly checked the draft, which was delaying the task; agreed to read it once and choose a planned send time.
Patient worked on a short draft message about a possible gradual return to work and had stopped before sending it.
No urgent safety concern was reported.
Patient reported one night of improved sleep followed by a night of prolonged wakefulness.
Rowan described concern that seeing outstanding work items would become overwhelming.
The team is helping Rowan break a difficult task into a manageable first step, and avoidance will be addressed in therapy.
Rowan asked for help understanding whom to contact about a gradual return to work schedule.
Patient worried about being asked for commitments they might not be able to meet after the supervisor's request.
Patient anticipated becoming overwhelmed if several work issues were raised at once.
Clinical presentation remained consistent with ongoing anxiety, low mood, and functional difficulty around work demands.
Patient kept postponing choosing a time for the conversation and was hesitant to complete the task outside the office.
No current suicidal ideation was reported.
Sleep remained uneven, with difficulty settling on nights when work-related thoughts became repetitive.
Repetitive planning at night affected settling for sleep.
Patient cancelled the individual appointment citing a personal scheduling conflict.
Rowan reported opening the work calendar but delaying a follow-up conversation.
Rowan remained anxious about the work conversation but could explain the intended first step.
Anxiety remained noticeable when anticipating contact with work.
A reminder about contacting work led to lengthy discussion, after which Rowan withdrew from the task.
Persistent avoidance; continues to delay follow-up on tasks.
Rowan reported that having a limited plan felt more manageable.
Meaningful functional impact around returning to work; trouble sustaining usual activities.
Mood felt less persistently low than earlier in the month.
Fewer days of pervasive low mood than reported at intake, per the questionnaire.
Partner described uncertainty about when reminders helped and when they increased Rowan's sense of pressure.
The patient denied current suicidal thoughts; no new acute safety issue emerged.
Sleep was still variable.
Sleep disruption remains an intermittent barrier to a steadier daytime routine.
